passage:
At the students’ union meeting in the small college hall, Pankaj stood up and proposed a shared cycle stand and a bicycle-lending scheme for students who travel from distant villages. Someone laughed. “Cycles? We want a canteen!” More laughter came from the back, and Pankaj sat down, red-faced.
I’m Kavitha, and I was near the front. I didn’t laugh. I raised my hand and asked, “How many students come from that far, and how do they get here now?”
Pankaj stood up again and said, “Almost forty. Many walk an hour.” The hall went silent. The chair wrote the number down.

qa.q: What did Pankaj propose at the meeting?
qa.a: Pankaj proposed a shared cycle stand and a bicycle-lending scheme for students who travel from distant villages.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have been feeling when the hall laughed at Pankaj?
qa.a: Kavitha probably felt uncomfortable with the laughter and curious about the idea, which is why Kavitha did not laugh and asked a real question instead.

qa.q: Why was Kavitha's follow-up question useful?
qa.a: It gave Pankaj a chance to explain with a real number and it showed respect for the idea. The answer changed how the hall reacted.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have thought when the chair wrote the number down?
qa.a: Pankaj might have felt relieved and heard for the first time, though the passage does not say what Pankaj thought.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing a majority laughing off a minority idea, and quiet follow-up questions revealing its worth.

passage:
In the seminar room in Manchester, Jamal suggested that the group’s project should look at night-shift workers at the station. Two classmates smirked. “Dull,” said one. “Nobody reads that stuff,” said another. The rest looked at their phones.
I’m Layla, and I was next to Jamal. He didn’t argue. He turned a page in his notebook and looked at the table.
“What would we ask them?” I said. Jamal blinked. Then he described three questions about sleep and safety on the way home. Two classmates stopped smirking.
“That’s actually good,” one said quietly. Jamal wrote something down and did not look up.

qa.q: Where did the group meet?
qa.a: The group met in a seminar room in Manchester.

qa.q: What might Layla have been feeling when the classmates smirked at Jamal?
qa.a: Layla was probably uncomfortable with the smirking and wanted Jamal's idea to get a fair hearing, so Layla asked a question instead of taking a side.

qa.q: Why did Layla's question change the mood?
qa.a: Layla did not take a side but asked what the group would ask the workers. It let Jamal explain his idea, and it showed that the idea was worth listening to.

qa.q: How might Jamal have felt when a classmate said his idea was actually good?
qa.a: Jamal may have felt relieved and quietly pleased. Writing something down and not looking up suggests he was moved but not showy.

grounding: Shows an observer seeing a majority laugh off a minority opinion, and a quiet follow-up question revealing a good point.

passage: In the engineering design lab, a team of eight was choosing a project for the college fest. Most wanted a drone. Noor, the only first-year, said quietly, 'What about a cheap water filter for the hostel taps?' Somebody snorted. 'Boring.' The talk rolled back to drones. Amandeep noticed Noor's face close up. Amandeep waited for a gap and asked, 'Noor, why the water filter?' Noor explained: half the hostel fell sick every monsoon, and the filter could be built from lab scraps for almost nothing. The room went quiet. 'That's actually useful,' someone admitted. In the end they did both: a small drone team and a filter team. Noor led the filter. It won the fest's Real-World Impact prize.

qa.q: What did Noor suggest?
qa.a: A cheap water filter for the hostel taps.

qa.q: What made Amandeep ask Noor a question?
qa.a: Amandeep noticed Noor's face close up and felt concerned that the idea had been dismissed without being heard.

qa.q: How did Amandeep's follow-up question help the team?
qa.a: It gave Noor room to explain, revealing a useful project the majority had laughed off.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when the idea was called boring?
qa.a: Small and dismissed as the only first-year, which is why Noor's face closed up.

grounding: A student notices the majority laughing off a minority idea and, by asking a follow-up question, reveals its value.

passage:
Dear Jagdish sir,
You asked us to notice how groups make decisions, so here's something from our tutorial. When we discussed whether to move the college festival online, twenty of us wanted it in person. Rinchen said online would let students from the hill villages join, since many can't afford the bus fare. Everyone laughed: 'Online fests are dead.' Rinchen stopped talking.
I didn't laugh, but I didn't speak either. Afterwards I found Rinchen and asked more. Rinchen told me eleven students from the hill hostels had missed last year's fest.
At the next tutorial, I asked the group to hear Rinchen out properly. We ended up planning a live stream as well as the in-person fest.
I'm still annoyed at myself for staying quiet the first time.
Dolma

qa.q: How many students from the hill hostels missed last year's fest?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How does Dolma feel about the first tutorial?
qa.a: Dolma feels annoyed and a bit ashamed about not speaking up when the class laughed.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that showed respect for the minority view?
qa.a: Found Rinchen afterwards, asked follow-up questions, and asked the group to hear Rinchen out properly.

qa.q: How might Rinchen have felt when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Dismissed and embarrassed, which is why Rinchen stopped talking.

grounding: A student notices the class laughing off a minority view and, by listening and asking questions, helps reveal its good point.

passage: Kavitha, since your podcast is about student life, here's one. I'm Chaitanya, final year. In our hostel meeting about the mess menu, one guy, Sonam, said the mess should label food with its ingredients because of allergies. Forty people laughed. Someone shouted, 'Next you'll want the menu in French!' Sonam went silent. I almost laughed too. Instead, after the meeting, I asked Sonam, 'What happened that made you say that?' It turned out Sonam's roommate had eaten something with peanuts and ended up in hospital. Nobody at the meeting knew. At the next meeting I asked Sonam to tell the story. Nobody laughed that time. The mess now puts up an ingredients board. I learned more from one question than from forty laughs.

qa.q: What did Sonam suggest the mess should do?
qa.a: Label food with its ingredients because of allergies.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling as the forty people laughed?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt uneasy about the crowd's laughter and curious about Sonam's reason.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya's follow-up question reveal?
qa.a: That Sonam's roommate had ended up in hospital after eating peanuts, a serious reason the majority had missed.

qa.q: How might Sonam have felt when forty people laughed?
qa.a: Humiliated and silenced, unable to explain a real safety worry.

grounding: A student notices the majority laugh off a minority suggestion and, by asking a follow-up question, reveals a good reason.

passage: I'm Mridul, and I was at the back of the planning meeting when it happened. Six of us were deciding our stall for the college fest, and everyone wanted the big food stall again. Nikita, who had hardly spoken all term, said, "What if we do a repair stall instead? Phones, cycles, zips." Someone snorted. Aman said, "Repair? At a fest?" and the others laughed and moved on to the menu. Nikita looked down at her notebook. I wasn't sure she was right either, but it bothered me how fast the idea got buried. So when the menu talk paused, I asked, "Nikita, why repair?" She explained: last year there were four food stalls, and all of them made a loss; the hostel had a queue for the one cycle-repair man every Sunday. The table went quiet. Aman said slowly, "Okay. That's actually smart."

qa.q: What kind of stall did Nikita suggest?
qa.a: A repair stall for phones, cycles and zips.

qa.q: Why did Mridul ask Nikita a follow-up question?
qa.a: Mridul was bothered and uneasy at how quickly her idea was buried, even without being sure it was right.

qa.q: What did Mridul's question show about listening to a lone view?
qa.a: Asking "why" gave Nikita room to explain, and her reasons about last year's stalls and the Sunday queue turned out to be a good point.

qa.q: How might Nikita have felt when the others laughed?
qa.a: She likely felt dismissed and embarrassed, looking down at her notebook, and then relieved when someone asked her to explain.

grounding: Mridul notices the majority laughing off a lone idea and, by asking a follow-up question, lets it reveal a good point.
